prompt: A team lead asks for the test plan to list every case the testers will run. What does lesson 1 say happens to such a plan?

choices.text: It becomes the strategy, and each project then refers to it
choices.why: A strategy is the organisation's standing "how", not a list of cases.

choices.text: It is the right size for a small team
choices.why: Size is not the objection; the cases change too often.

choices.text: It is out of date by the second day
choices.why: Right: cases change with every requirement, and the decisions above them change far less.

choices.text: It satisfies ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3, which asks for a list of cases in the plan
choices.why: The standard's list of plan contents reads as seven questions, and the cases are not one of them.

prompt: Lesson 1 ranks risk D, "the confirmation e-mail never arrives", as medium impact rather than high. What is the reason it gives?

choices.text: E-mail is out of scope for this release, so its impact is never judged
choices.why: The real mail server is out of scope; the e-mail itself is risk D.

choices.text: The customer still books, just without the member discount
choices.why: Right: the harm is a lost discount, not a lost sale.

choices.text: The developers think it is unlikely
choices.why: That is likelihood, which is judged separately and is low here.

choices.text: An e-mail costs nothing to send again
choices.why: Resending is a feature; impact is about the harm when it fails.

prompt: Ana starts testing a build whose environment does not answer yet, ignoring the entry criteria. By lesson 1, what does her first day produce?

choices.text: A list of defects that Rui can fix the same afternoon

choices.text: A signed-off exit report

choices.text: Reports about the environment that nobody can act on
choices.why: Right: failures about the environment rather than the product.

choices.text: Scenarios carry the expected results that the cases then copy word for word

choices.text: Because a scenario and a case are the same thing

choices.text: The duplicate sign-up goes through

choices.text: Asking the writer which state they meant

A test suite pins the clock with BOXOFFICE_NOW for every test. What can such a suite never show?

choices.text: Whether booking for a show really closes an hour before it starts
choices.why: That is exactly what the fake clock makes easy.

choices.text: Anything that depends on where the machine is in the world
choices.why: Right: lesson 21 shows such a defect.

choices.text: Whether a student pays half
choices.why: The price rule does not read the clock.

choices.text: Whether sign-up sends an e-mail
choices.why: The mock of send checks that.

prompt: Ordinary load held for hours, to find what only shows over time, such as memory that is never given back, is called soak or ___ testing.
Every boxoffice page answers with a Server header naming the exact Python version. How does lesson 14 rate it?

choices.text: Minor, and worth a line in a report
choices.why: Right: many teams remove or blur it in production.

choices.text: Harmless, since it is not a password
choices.why: It is free knowledge for an attacker, if small.

choices.text: The very same defect as the traceback
choices.why: It is a smaller detail on every page, a separate line.

choices.text: A breach of R7
choices.why: R7 is about answering wrong input; this is a header on every page.

prompt: A stress test pushes boxoffice past its peak. Why does lesson 14 care how it fails, and not only where?

choices.text: Because the point where it fails is the same on every machine
choices.why: The point depends on the machine; that is why it is measured.

choices.text: Because only a crash counts as failing
choices.why: Slowing down past a promised time is a failure too.

choices.text: Because load tools report nothing else
choices.why: They record every response time and every error.

choices.text: A system that slows and recovers is better off than one that loses orders
choices.why: Right: the way it fails is part of the finding.

prompt: After Caio signs up with 12345678, Ana counts the lines of the outbox that hold that password. Which result would be a defect?

choices.text: A count of 0
choices.why: That is the result she got, and the right one.

choices.text: Any count above 0: the password sent back
choices.why: Right: a password in an e-mail is a defect.

choices.text: An outbox with no e-mail at all
choices.why: That would be a sign-up that sent no confirmation, a different finding.

choices.text: The account being created with a weak password
choices.why: R2 allows it; that is a question for the client.

prompt: Which defect does lesson 15 give as critical and still low priority?

choices.text: The 760-pixel shows table that phone customers scroll
choices.why: That is minor and P1, the opposite combination.

choices.text: The student discount on 1.1, which overcharges students
choices.why: Critical and P1: every student is overcharged now.

choices.text: The misspelt "cannot be useed"
choices.why: Trivial, not critical.

choices.text: A crash in a season not on sale until next year
choices.why: Right: no customer meets it before it is fixed.

prompt: A report ends: "the int() call needs a try/except". What does lesson 15 say is wrong with that line?

choices.text: It starts fixing code its writer does not own, by guessing
choices.why: Right: a guessed cause misleads about half the time; the traceback names the line and the developer reads it there.

choices.text: It belongs in the title, not at the end
choices.why: It belongs nowhere in the report.

choices.text: It should name the line number
choices.why: The traceback already does; the guess is the problem.

choices.text: Nothing: a suggested fix saves the developer time on every report
choices.why: A guessed cause is a fix nobody asked the tester for.

prompt: Ana thinks a minor defect should be fixed sooner. What does lesson 15 tell her to do?

choices.text: Mark it critical so that triage notices it
choices.why: Triage then reads all her severities with a discount.

choices.text: Set the priority to P1 herself, in the report
choices.why: Priority is hers to suggest and someone else's to decide.

choices.text: Argue for it in a sentence in the report
choices.why: Right: that is an argument about priority, made where it belongs.

choices.text: File it twice so that it counts double at triage
choices.why: Duplicates cost triage time and change nothing.

prompt: After triage, when does lesson 15 say a defect's severity changes?

choices.text: When a deadline moves
choices.why: That moves priority.

choices.text: When something new is learnt about the harm
choices.why: Right: for example the traceback turning up on a page every customer uses.

choices.text: When a customer complains about it on the phone
choices.why: A complaint moves the cost of waiting, which is priority.

choices.text: When the fix turns out to be cheap and quick to make
choices.why: Cost of the fix is a priority matter.

prompt: A retest fails. Why does lesson 16 reopen the report rather than file a new one?

choices.text: A new report would have to go through the whole triage again, a week of waiting
choices.why: The reason is the history, not the queue.

choices.text: The tracker cannot hold two reports on one page
choices.why: Any tracker can.

choices.text: The history stays attached, and the defect does not look younger than it is
choices.why: Right: the developer sees what was tried and why it did not hold.

choices.text: Reopening raises the defect's severity
choices.why: Severity moves with the harm, not the state.

prompt: Which of these is an escaped defect, by lesson 16?

choices.text: One a customer meets on opening night
choices.why: Right: found by a customer after the release.

choices.text: One the manager finds in the acceptance session
choices.why: That is still before release, by the client.

choices.text: One that a retest of the fix sends back reopened
choices.why: That counts in the reopen rate.

choices.text: One that triage deferred to the next release
choices.why: A deferred defect is known and decided.

prompt: Why does lesson 16 call a chart of total open defects, with no severity, theatre?

choices.text: Because open defects cannot be counted reliably
choices.why: They can; the count hides what matters.

choices.text: Because it goes up whenever testers work
choices.why: That is the per-tester count's problem.

choices.text: Because charts belong in lesson 19
choices.why: Where it is drawn is not the objection.

choices.text: Thirty misspellings closed and the refund left open look like progress
choices.why: Right: a falling total says nothing about what fell.

prompt: Lesson 16 says a rejection is a sentence, never a bare ___: "Rejected" alone tells the reporter they were wrong and not why.
Two defects are filed in one tracker issue. What goes wrong, by lesson 17?

choices.text: They share one id, one state and one history, so they cannot be closed separately
choices.why: Right: fixing one closes both.

choices.text: The tracker refuses a second attachment
choices.why: Attachments are not limited to one.

choices.text: Search finds the issue twice
choices.why: It finds it once, which is the trouble.

choices.text: The board shows two cards
choices.why: One issue is one card.

prompt: Rui's commit message carries the key BOX-42, and the code lives in Bitbucket. What does that give Ana when she retests BOX-42?

choices.text: An automatic verified state on the issue
choices.why: Verifying is the tester's move.

choices.text: A copy of the test plan for the release
choices.why: Plans live on the wiki.

choices.text: She sees exactly what changed
choices.why: Right: the issue shows the commit, because the key links code to issue.

choices.text: A new severity field on the issue
choices.why: Fields are added by an administrator.

prompt: A customer's help-desk request in Jira Service Management turns out to be a defect. What is it to a tester, by lesson 17?

choices.text: A request to close as rejected, since customers do not file defects
choices.why: Customers find defects; that is the point.

choices.text: The front door of the escaped defects lesson 16 counted
choices.why: Right: found by a customer after release.

choices.text: A duplicate of the newest report
choices.why: Nothing says it was reported before.

choices.text: A change request for the wiki
choices.why: The wiki holds pages, not requests.

prompt: Feature lists make Jira, Trello, YouTrack and Assembla look alike. Lesson 17 says what separates them is what each one ___.
Besides issues, fields, a workflow, a board and search, what does lesson 17 say every one of its trackers also does? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Keeps a history of who changed which field, and when
choices.why: Right: that is how a reopened defect carries its past.

choices.text: Links issues to each other
choices.why: Right: a duplicate points at its original.

choices.text: Restricts who can see an issue
choices.why: Right: where a security report goes.

choices.text: Sets each defect's priority from its severity
choices.why: Priority is set at triage by people.

choices.text: Writes a description template for every new bug
choices.why: The team agrees the template; some trackers only start a bug with it.

prompt: A team keeps two thousand cases in Zephyr, inside the same Jira project as its work. What does lesson 18 say that costs?

choices.text: A licence per case
choices.why: No price is quoted, and pricing per case is not the point.

choices.text: The link between a failed execution and its bug
choices.why: That link is the attraction: both live in one tool.

choices.text: Many issues for everybody else to filter out, and cases that move wherever Jira goes
choices.why: Right: the case model takes the tracker's shape.

choices.text: A server to install and back up
choices.why: That is TestLink's cost.

prompt: Excel set up for Portuguese opens cases.csv with everything in column A. What does lesson 18 say to do?

choices.text: Import it, choosing the comma as the delimiter
choices.why: Right: that Excel expects a semicolon.

choices.text: Replace every comma in the file with a semicolon by hand
choices.why: Commas inside the quoted steps would break.

choices.text: Switch Excel to English for the day
choices.why: Not what the lesson says.

choices.text: Save it again as .xlsx before opening
choices.why: It has to open properly first.

prompt: In a spreadsheet of cases, each run is a column. Three releases, each run on lesson 7's four browsers: how many run columns is that?
Which job does lesson 18 say a case tool does not do?

choices.text: Keep each case's results across every run
choices.why: That is its results history.

choices.text: Link a failed result to the defect it caused
choices.why: That is its traceability.

choices.text: Group cases into suites by area of the product
choices.why: That is its repository.

choices.text: Write the cases, or choose them
choices.why: Right: that is lessons 3 and 10's work.

prompt: Why does the page for 1.1 open with "Not ready to release" rather than "some concerns, mostly passing"?

choices.text: Leadership is not allowed to read anything softer
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; the reason is how it is read.

choices.text: A softened answer is read as a yes
choices.why: Right: the answer is a word, in the first row.

choices.text: The tester decides the release
choices.why: The decision is the manager's; the page informs it.

choices.text: Most of the cases failed on 1.1, so the word had to be strong
choices.why: Ten of seventeen passed; the answer comes from the exit criteria.

prompt: Allure marks a test that passed on a retry after failing, a test whose result cannot be trusted on a single run, as ___.
Nobody reads JUnit XML for pleasure. What does lesson 19 say is its value?

choices.text: It is the format leadership reads first
choices.why: Leadership reads one page.

choices.text: It records blocked cases as a result of their own
choices.why: Blocked has no element of its own.

choices.text: It is a published standard every tool follows exactly
choices.why: Nobody published it; tools differ at the edges.

choices.text: It is boring and shared, so tools that know nothing of boxoffice read a run
choices.why: Right: the hand-over between what ran the tests and what shows them.

prompt: cases.csv has 17 cases. On 1.0, three were not run and five failed. How many passed on 1.0?
A tester's one-page report runs to three pages. Where does lesson 19 say the excess usually is?

choices.text: In the exit criteria, which should be summarised
choices.why: They are quoted from the plan, each with a yes or a no.

choices.text: In the numbers row
choices.why: The numbers are one line, each saying what it counts.

choices.text: In the second row, describing every defect
choices.why: Right: keep those that change the decision and link the rest.

choices.text: In the answer, which needs a paragraph of context
choices.why: The answer is a word or a short sentence.

prompt: Why is data from make_accounts.py not realistic by default, by lesson 20?

choices.text: A generator produces exactly the variety it was written to produce
choices.why: Right: real customers paste spaces and type one-word names.

choices.text: Its names have accents
choices.why: The accents are there on purpose, to test the name field.

choices.text: Its addresses are numbered
choices.why: Numbering keeps them apart; it is not the realism question.

choices.text: Its seed changes every run
choices.why: The seed is fixed, which makes every run the same.

prompt: Why does lesson 20 call restoring the database before the run the most trustworthy of the three ways back?

choices.text: It needs no saved state to be kept up to date
choices.why: It does: somebody keeps the saved state current.

choices.text: It is the fastest of the three
choices.why: Speed is not the reason given.

choices.text: Each case then makes its own data
choices.why: That is a different approach.

choices.text: It does not depend on the last run finishing properly
choices.why: Right: a run that fails halfway leaves a mess for cleanup to miss.

prompt: Hamlet starts with 80 seats and is never reset. A case books six Hamlet tickets each time it runs. On which run does it first fail for lack of seats?
A masked copy shows D***** B****** beside a city and a birth date. Why can it still be personal data in practice?

choices.text: Masking can be undone by removing the asterisks
choices.why: The letters are gone; nothing brings them back.

choices.text: An initial and a length, beside other columns, may be enough to recognise somebody
choices.why: Right: among a small theatre's members.

choices.text: The key used for masking may leak
choices.why: Masking uses no key; pseudonymising does.

choices.text: Masked rows still join between tables
choices.why: They do not; that is the property masking loses.

prompt: Why is development a poor environment to test in, by lesson 21?

choices.text: It holds real customers' data, which testers must not see
choices.why: That is production; development holds whatever the developer typed.

choices.text: It changes constantly: the code moves under the report
choices.why: Right: a test environment runs a known build.

choices.text: It sends e-mail to real people
choices.why: Development rarely sends e-mail at all.

choices.text: Testers are not allowed to use the developers' own laptops
choices.why: Permission is not the reason given.

prompt: Staging must not hold real customers' data, so it differs from production there. Where does lesson 21 say such a gap is recorded?

choices.text: Nowhere: parity gaps are expected and need no note
choices.why: An unrecorded gap is the dangerous kind.

choices.text: In each defect report that touches it
choices.why: Reports record the environment of one run, not the team's decisions.

choices.text: In the production server's logs
choices.why: Logs record requests, not decisions.

choices.text: In the test plan, next to the reason
choices.why: Right: so a defect hiding there is a known risk.

prompt: Put the four environments in order, from the furthest from what customers use to what they use.
How much of a machine belongs in a report's environment block, by lesson 21?

choices.text: What could plausibly differ between your machine and the reader's
choices.why: Right: versions, zone, language, how it was started, the data.

choices.text: Every setting the machine has, to be safe
choices.why: A page of settings hides the line that matters.

choices.text: Only the application's version
choices.why: Defect 9 needed the zone and how it was started.

choices.text: Whatever the tester suspects matters for this particular defect, and no more
choices.why: Recording it only when suspected is the wrong habit.

prompt: A defect shows on one machine and not on another. What does lesson 21 ask the report to say?

choices.text: The failing machine only, since that is where the defect is
choices.why: Then the reader has to rediscover the passing one.

choices.text: That it cannot be reproduced by the developer
choices.why: It can, on the failing side.

choices.text: Both, closed on UTC and open in São Paulo
choices.why: Right: closed on UTC, open on America/Sao_Paulo, same instant tells Rui where to look before he reads on.

choices.text: The developer's machine settings, which the tester asks for
choices.why: The tester reproduces both on one machine instead.

prompt: Why does a confirmation token expire, by lesson 22?

choices.text: A link that never expired would be a secret forever
choices.why: Right: sitting in an inbox for years.

choices.text: To keep the outbox small
choices.why: The outbox keeps everything until a restart.

choices.text: Because the member discount itself ends after 24 hours
choices.why: The discount stays with a confirmed account.

choices.text: Because mail servers delete any link after a full day
choices.why: Mail servers do not touch the link.

prompt: Restarting boxoffice with BOXOFFICE_NOW cannot test expiry. Which test does lesson 22 give as honest?

choices.text: Restart with the clock 25 hours ahead and open the old link
choices.why: The restart wipes the link, so the refusal measures nothing.

choices.text: Change one character of the token
choices.why: That is case 2, a token nobody issued.

choices.text: Leave it running on the real clock and open links after 23 and 25 hours
choices.why: Right: it takes a day and it is a real test.

choices.text: Ask for a new link and open the old one
choices.why: That is case 4, replacement rather than expiry.

prompt: Many products refuse sign-ups at known disposable domains such as Mailinator's. What does that mean for a team that tests with it?

choices.text: Nothing; the refusal only applies in production
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says it waits for production.

choices.text: If meant to, the refusal is a requirement and a case
choices.why: Right: and if not, the team finds out the day it starts.

choices.text: The team switches to real customers' addresses instead
choices.why: Never real people's data in a test.

choices.text: Mailinator stops delivering the confirmation messages
choices.why: Mailinator still receives; the product is the one refusing.

prompt: On a fresh start, Caio signs up, Dora signs up, and Dora asks for a new link. How many messages does the outbox hold?
Which of these are true of MailHog and Mailpit? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: They pretend to be a mail server and keep every message
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They show the caught messages on a web page
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: They forward a copy to the real inbox as well
choices.why: Nothing is delivered anywhere.

choices.text: They prove a real mail server would deliver the message
choices.why: That is their limit: delivery is invisible to them.

choices.text: The application's mail settings are pointed at them instead of the real server
choices.why: Right: the settings are part of the environment.
